title: Aph. XIX-XXII: practical part (Acts); epistolary part; Paul's fourteen letters
pass_a_gloss: Pass A clause gloss: one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, one to the Ephesians, one to the Philippians, one to the Colossians, two to the Thessalonians, two to Timothy, one to Titus, one to Philemon, one to the Hebrews. Paul wrote these by name: XXII. The Apostolic epistles were written partly by Paul — namely fourteen — partly by James — namely one — partly by Peter — namely two — partly by John — namely three — partly by Jude — namely one. XXI. written by the Apostles in epistolary character concerning the chief heads belonging toward Christian religion plus the very practice belonging toward Christian faith plus life in truth, according to the measure belonging toward each one's gift plus calling, to be exercised by anyone in the course belonging toward this pilgrimage until the world's end — written to those absent from the Old Testament, Christ's sermons, plus the Holy Spirit's suggestion — the epistolary stands as the third part belonging toward the New Testament. XX. written by Luke at Rome by the will belonging toward Paul the prisoner — concerning the birth plus infancy, growth, plus just, gracious, plus most simple face, teaching, strength, plus whole form belonging toward government belonging toward the optimally constituted primitive Church belonging toward Christ plus belonging toward reunion, plus concerning the deeds belonging toward the Apostles fighting against false doctrine, described under the face plus condition belonging toward the Ephesian Church (Revelation 2:1) — the practical stands as the second part. XIX.
pass_b_english: XIX. The practical is the second part, written by Luke at Rome by the will of Paul the prisoner — concerning the birth and infancy, growth, and just, gracious, and most simple face, teaching, strength, and whole form of government of the optimally constituted primitive Church of Christ and of reunion, and concerning the deeds of the Apostles fighting against false doctrine, described under the face and condition of the Ephesian Church ([[Revelation 2:1 >> Bible:Revelation 2:1]]).

XX. The epistolary is the third part of the New Testament, written by the Apostles in epistolary character concerning the chief heads of Christian religion and the very practice of Christian faith and life in truth, according to the measure of each one's gift and calling, to be exercised by anyone in the course of this pilgrimage until the world's end — written to those absent from the Old Testament, Christ's sermons, and the Holy Spirit's suggestion.
XXI. The Apostolic epistles were written partly by Paul — namely fourteen — partly by James — namely one — partly by Peter — namely two — partly by John — namely three — partly by Jude — namely one.

XXII. Paul wrote these by name: one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, one to the Ephesians, one to the Philippians, one to the Colossians, two to the Thessalonians, two to Timothy, one to Titus, one to Philemon, one to the Hebrews.
source_text: XIX. Practica est pars altera, a Luca Romae de voluntate Pauli vincti conscripta, de ortu & infantia, incrementis & justa grate simplicissimaque facie, doctrina, viribus, totiusque forma regimine optime constitutae primitivae Ecclesiae Christi & reunionis, deque gestis Apostolorum pugnantium contra falsam doctrinam, sub facie & conditione Ecclesiae Ephesinae, Apoc. 2.v.1. descriptis. XX. Epistolica est tertia pars N.T. ab Apostolis charactere epistolari scripta de summis religionis Christianae capitibus & ipsissima fidei vitaeque Christianae praxi veritate pro mensura doni & vocationis sua a quovis in curriculo hujus peregrinationis usque ad finem mundi exercenda ex veteri testamento, Christi concionibus, et Spiritus S. suggestione ad absentes scripta. XXI. Epistolae Apostolicae conscriptae sunt partim a Paulo, nempe quatuordecim, partim a Jacobo, nempe una, partim a Petro, nempe duae, partim a Johanne, nempe tres, partim a Juda, sc. una. XXII. Paulus nominatim has scripsit, unam ad Romanos, duas ad Corinthios, ad Galatas unam, ad Ephesios unam, ad Philippenses unam, ad Colossenses unam, ad Thessalonicenses duas, ad Timotheum duas, ad Titum unam, unam ad Philemonem, unam ad Hebraeos.
